Customs and excise divisions-
302. General administration, $2,105,832.

I think perhaps that if I made a brief explanatory statement with reference to the division of customs and excise it might make it unnecessary to ask a lot of questions which would otherwise be asked. This will only take two or three minutes.
The estimates now before the house are intended to cover operations of the customs and excise division of the Department of National Revenue, which consists of some 215 customs-excise ports, approximately 145 outports and other offices, as well as the central administration.
This division administers the customs tariff, the Customs Act, the Excise Tax Act, the Excise Act, and portions of some forty other acts. The ports and outports are responsible for the examination and appraisal of imported goods; the assessment and collection of duties and taxes payable thereon; the assessment and collection of excise duty, excise taxes and sales taxes on domestic goods; the supervision of customs bonded warehouses and of licensed excise establishments, and the administration of the laws mentioned above and regulations made thereunder.
Through headquarters and the ports special branches are staffed to carry out audits, inspections, investigations, drawbacks and refunds.
During the last year the department collected, by way of revenue, $1,476 million, an increase of $250 million over the previous year. The estimate of revenue for 1952-53, as projected by the Minister of Finance, will be in the neighbourhood of $1,495 million. The expected increase for this year has already been reflected in the revenue for April and May, and the indications are that the customs and excise division will again see an increase in the volume of business.

Supply-National Revenue
International traffic appears to be continuing on the upswing, especially in the fields of trucking and tourist travel. Foreign vehicles entering Canada on travellers' vehicle permits in the month of April totalled 56,400, an increase of 12 per cent over the previous year, and a new record for the month. Traffic has been heavier in all parts of the country, with the largest gains occurring in Ontario and Quebec. The four-month total from January to April is actually 9 per cent higher than it was for the corresponding period last year.
This year's estimates provide for an increase over last year of $1,999,153. The larger part, in fact 95 per cent of this increase, or in other words $1,914,126, is required to cover the adjustments in salary occasioned by the general increase applicable to all government employees, and for the addition of sufficient positions to bring us up to the same strength as last year.
Apart from the need for additional seasonal officers, provision is being made for an essential increase in the excise tax audit staff and the customs appraisers. Both these branches are now overworked. An increase of 25 auditors is essential, both for protection ' of the revenue and for better service to the taxpayers by more frequent audits. Excise tax auditors average an annual recovery of some $20,000 per auditor, and assist the taxpayers in a fuller understanding of the tax regulations. Seven new customs appraisers will be added to the department to cope with the problem of investigation of foreign values, about which I spoke to the house in the course of discussion of the customs tariff bill.
Other votes which show an increase over last year relate to overtime and office and bousing accommodation. Overtime, it will be noted, this year shows an apparent increase of $100,000 over last year. Actually the amount we are working for is $80,000 less than the amount we were required to expend last year. A substantial portion of overtime results from special services to the public and is recouped from persons so served. The moneys thus repaid to the government are placed in the consolidated revenue fund, and heretofore have not been credited against the departmental expenditures.
The department's estimate of amounts recovered is in the neighbourhood of $300,000 annually; therefore in the preparation of these estimates the amount of $300,000 has been deducted from the over-all vote for ports, outports and preventive stations so that, in effect, the department is seeking

$500,000 for overtime payments, expecting that the balance of its requirements will be obtained from those to whom special services are rendered. The vote covering construction and the acquisition of land this year shows an increase over last year of $243,450. In this connection I would like to say that the projects envisaged for the coming year are projects which have been regularly deferred until they are now of some urgency. There still remains a long list of other such projects which, although desirable, must be deferred still further. It should be remembered that all during the war and the period that followed a close check has been kept on construction, despite the fact that the volume of business and the local demands for service have greatly increased throughout these years.
I shall be pleased to answer any questions that may arise in connection with any of these estimates.

I do not
propose to take the time of the committee in making any general remarks, and shall confine myself to plunging at once into questions. The minister has given us a broad picture of the situation, with figures that are relevant. I should like to ask him whether it will suit him, on this item or on item 306, to deal with one question which I think exercises the mind of the public a good deal, namely the question of smuggling and enforcement. I am anxious to get a certain amount of detailed information about that. Some time ago the question was taken up with the Department of Justice, and we had a sort of general assertion from the Minister of Justice that the situation was improving, which was not as convincing as it might have been. I should like the minister to give us a considerable amount of detail. We have only about fifteen minutes left this evening, and if he would prefer to deal with that first thing in the morning I would be prepared to leave it until then.
If that is his wish, I should like to turn now to one or two other questions. Perhaps the minister would indicate his preference now. Shall we proceed immediately with the question of smuggling, or would the minister prefer to leave that until the first thing in the morning?
I think probably we might proceed in the regular way, Mr. Chairman. The practice that has been followed under the first item, general administration, is that almost any questions may be asked.
I am now asking a question, but I am in doubt as to whether the minister wants to proceed-
I am satisfied to have you go ahead with any questions you desire to ask.

First of all I should like to know what the minister considers was the loss to the treasury last year from smuggling operations. He will recall what the Minister of Finance said in his speech on April 8, as recorded at page 1258 of Hansard:
In the case of cigarettes only I had forecast an increase of $21 million and I experienced a decline of $1 million. There are of course a number of reasons for this decline.
There is also a statement which I shall read from a publication with which I am not very familiar, but which evidently went into this matter. It is the March 8 edition of Weekend picture magazine. I shall read from it quite briefly. This purports to give a picture of the smuggling situation:
When the federal government raised the tax on a package of cigarettes to 25-2 cents last April (the U.S. federal tax is eight cents) and the cigarette manufacturers followed up with price increases to bring the cost of a package of cigarettes to 42 cents (46 cents with provincial tax in Quebec), the petty smuggler faded into the background along the border as the big operators gradually went into the business. The men who became rich in prohibition days and those who wished to emulate them saw their opportunity. They could buy a carton of cigarettes in Maryland, where there is no state tax, for as little as $1.59 from distributors. This same carton brought from $3 to $3.50 on the Canadian black market-as much as 120 per cent profit. Buyers were easy to find, for the same number of Canadian cigarettes cost $4.20 in most provinces and $4.60 in Quebec.
Some idea of the quantities being moved surreptitiously into Canada may be gained from the fact that an R.C.M.P. patrol seized a cache of 970,000 cigarettes in a new three-ton truck on a farm near Coaticook last December 15. On the Canadian black market such a load is worth $14,550.
There is a lot more here I could read, but I do not want to lengthen these proceedings an unnecessary moment. I do want, however, to get from the minister what he considers the most significant facts. First of all I want to know the number of prosecutions and seizures which were being made prior to the change in the tax on April 8 last, and whether the minister has reason to think the situation has improved very greatly. Some opinions I have heard, though I cannot profess to have verified them, seem to indicate that the change is not nearly as great as one might expect.
I should like the minister to begin by telling us what he considers the loss to have been, in so far as he is informed; and second, the course of the prosecutions and police activity up until the time the tax was changed and since.

I shall admit, Mr. Chairman, that the matter of smuggling, particularly of
Supply-National Revenue cigarettes, has been a problem which has engaged the attention of the officials of the department, and given them considerable anxiety. If we go back a few years, I can give the total number of seizures. For the year 1951 there were 7,061. If we go back to 1945, we find that there were 2,697 seizures. It has gone up gradually, and in 1946 there were 4,482; in 1947, 4,835; 1948, 5,207; 1949, 5,655; 1950, 6,530; and in 1951, 7,061.
However, we find that the peak was reached in the month of September, when there were 731 seizures, and that declined until December of 1951, when it was reduced to 644. I think perhaps it might be interesting if I gave you something specific with reference to the seizure of cigarettes; that is, cigarettes seized by police and the ports in the years 1949, 1950 and 1951. Perhaps the last few months would interest you, or give you a comparison with a year ago. In June of 1951 there were 1,241,284 cigarettes seized. The peak, as I said, was reached at the first of this year, in January of 1952, when the number was 1,889,290; and it has been gradually going down since January. If you take the month of May, the seizures were then 1,139,160.
That is the number of cigarettes. How many seizures were there?
How many what?
The minister has given the total seized, as I understand it.
Yes. Then I was giving you specifically the figures for cigarettes. I think that is what you wanted. I believe this might help to clear up the situation.

Can the
minister give the number of seizures in May of this year?
May of last year?

No; May of
this year.
Yes. Of cigarettes, 1,139,160.
That is the number of cigarettes seized?

That is the number of
cigarettes.
Yes; but what was the number of seizures?
The number of seizures? In May, 1951, it was 600 and in May, 1952, it was 707.

Then do I understand that actually the number of seizures in May of 1952 was worse than in 1951, although the tax had been reduced in April?
4228	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Revenue We would not expect that results would appear immediately perhaps; but it is certainly disconcerting to find the situation was worse this last May than it was a year ago.
In May, 1952 the number was 707; but the peak in 1951 was in September of that year when there were 731 seizures.
May I point out to the minister that that peak of September, 1951, if I have the figures down correctly, was 731 seizures whereas in May of 1952 we have 770. In other words the situation is worse.
I hope the hon. gentleman will understand that is 731 seizures of everything.
When did we shift over from cigarettes?
I wanted to give you specifically the number of cigarettes, but I have not the information here as to the number of seizures of cigarettes.

May I ask this question. After all, if we are going to have any real appreciation of what is going on we must have comparable figures. I think it is clear that what we need are comparable figures running right through in order to show whether this thing is getting better or worse. It is not merely a matter of the money lost; it is the whole unpleasant disregard of law. What I mean is this. Once people get into the habit of disobeying one law, they can easily extend the habit. May I now suggest that this item might stand until the morning.
If the hon. member will give me an opportunity to answer the rest of his question, perhaps he would have the information. He asked a question with reference to the money.

I always like the minister better when he is good tempered. Do not let him and me fall out with each other. What we are actually finding is that the minister was giving figures that were not comparable, and I do not think they were getting us anywhere. If he has other comparable figures that he wants to give us, I should be glad to have them. But I am suggesting that, at the moment, we are comparing things that are not comparable. If the minister wants to go on, I am perfectly willing to do so.

I think perhaps if I were to give this statement it might help to clarify the situation. It has to do both with cigarettes and tobacco.
Although it is somewhat early as yet to assess the effect of the recent lowering of the


tax on cigarettes-and I think that is the information the hon. member wanted-it can be reported that there has been a falling off in the quantities of cigarettes seized since the budget. Cigarettes seized during the month of May amount to 1,139,000. This is some 360,000 less than the number seized in the previous month-that would be April- and almost 1 million less than the peak reached in November last.
A further indication that the situation has improved is perhaps evidenced by the increase in the production of Canadian cigarettes which, for the month of April, shows an increase of 100 million over April of last year-the figures are 1,523 million compared with 1,438 million-and the May figures which show an increase over the corresponding month of last year of 284 million.
The revenue figures for cigarettes present a similar comparative picture for the month of May, and show an increase this year of $927,000. The amount collected in May of this year also exceeds the revenue collected in May of 1950 by over half a million dollars.
Is that both customs and excise?

No. There is not much customs collected on cigarettes; it is excise tax and excise duty. I was giving the comparative figures. The amount collected in May of this year exceeds that collected in May of 1950 by half a million dollars, the figures being $15,359,000 as compared with $14,855,000 a year ago.
The production figures for cut tobacco are perhaps even more impressive, the months of April and May showing an increase over the same period last year of 1,162,000 pounds. That is the production of cut tobacco.

Those production figures have their own interest, but you would need to know a great deal about them in order to know what their real bearing is on smuggling. The mere fact that we are producing a great deal more than we were producing before might mean that there was an arrears of production and that they were speeding up. I come back to this point. I want to know the number of seizures. To me it is not of great importance, if the number of seizures is going up, that the actual average amount seized is less. I do not regard that fact as of great importance. That perhaps means that they are not operating on quite as large a scale, but still they are operating. I see that it is now eleven o'clock. I would therefore suggest that in the morning the minister might give us a list of the seizures running back over a good many months, say over the last eighteen months.
Does the hon. member mean seizures of everything, including cars, cigarettes and jewelry?

Either of everything or of cigarettes. I started with cigarettes. If the minister will give us comparative figures, and if those relating to cigarettes are most convenient, I suggest he give us the figures for cigarettes. It will be quite satisfactory to me if we can get a figure carried through that is comparable so we can form, an estimate of what is going on.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
